proof:
# Recovery from transformed component meshes

This is a conditional recovery theorem. The original mesh divided by
the original coarse mass need not tend to zero. Instead the fine
lattices must become dense AFTER block-preserving shape normalization
in every retained positive-mass component. Those transformed meshes
can fail to become dense, as the exact crossed-triangle example shows.
No OC theorem is applied to a fine auxiliary set with varying cosets
and covolumes; all fine estimates below are direct sampling estimates.

## 1. Setting and theorem

Let k>=0, r>=1, s>=0 and m=r+s. Write coordinates (z,u,x) in
R^k times R^r times R^s. Let P subset Z^k be finite, lattice-convex,
and spanning R^k. Let K_(l,z) subset R^r times R^s be actual
compatible full m-dimensional coarse fibers, with

    M_l=sum_z |K_(l,z)|,
    |K_(l,z)|/M_l -> p_z>0 for every z in P.             (1)

The fine base is one original lattice coset Lambda_l+a_l in R^r,
with covolume v_l. The original fine measure is

    mu_l=v_l sum_(z in P, u in Lambda_l+a_l)
                      H_s restricted to (K_(l,z))_u.     (2)

For s=0, H_0 counts a point. Write P_1,...,P_c for the finite
dependence components of P. Construct the compact full-shape lift
from `candidate c344f12be982dcb7`,
using component maps of the BLOCK form

    T_(l,i)(u,x)=(A_(l,i)u, B_(l,i)u+C_(l,i)x),
    |det A_(l,i) det C_(l,i)|=1/M_l.                    (3)

Section 2 shows that such block maps are always available for the
shape compactification. They do NOT automatically make the fine
lattices dense. The additional hypothesis of this theorem is

    rho_(l,i):=covering radius of A_(l,i)Lambda_l ->0
                          for EVERY component i.         (4)

After taking the full-shape subsequence, let B_* be its compact
intrinsic lift limit, with normalized intrinsic H_m law nu_*.
Then the original normalized fine depths satisfy

    liminf_l max depth_(mu_l) >= max depth_(nu_*).        (5)

The actual fine mass is positive eventually. Every recovery point
in the proof belongs to the ORIGINAL fine set, with its original
coarse integer base and its original fine lattice coordinates.

## 2. Block-preserving compact shape normalization

Start with any component anchor normalization S_(l,i) used in the
full-shape lift, with |det S_(l,i)|=1/M_l. It gives bounded anchor
shape and, by incidence propagation, bounded diameters throughout
that component. Let V={0} times R^s be the continuous subspace.
Choose an orthogonal map O_(l,i) carrying the s-dimensional space
S_(l,i)V onto V. Then T_(l,i)=O_(l,i)S_(l,i) preserves V, hence has
the block form (3). Orthogonality changes neither its absolute
determinant nor its diameter bounds. Both diagonal blocks in (3)
are invertible. If s=0 the condition is vacuous and det C is one.

For z in component i, set

    R_(l,z)=T_(l,i)K_(l,z)-g_(l,z),                     (6)

where the bounded-position correction g_l has every coordinate in
L(P), as in the full-shape theorem. All R_(l,z) lie in one fixed
ball, have volumes |K_(l,z)|/M_l, remain compatible, and converge
along a subsequence to positive full m-dimensional bodies R_z.
Each coordinate of g_l is allowed to be representation-affine;
it need not be an ordinary affine function of z.

The fixed orthogonal component blocks and fixed continuous graph
features of that theorem give actual convex lifts B_l. Denote their
intrinsic volume laws by nu_l; each has total mass one. Their global
affine maps F_l fix the coarse base and act on component i, fiber z,
as T_(l,i)^(-1)(w+g_(l,z)). They push nu_l to the original coarse
volume divided by M_l.

### 2.1 The mesh condition is independent of the round block frame

Suppose T and T_tilde are two block-preserving maps for the SAME
component anchor, and their translated anchor images contain balls
of radii rho,rho_tilde>0 and are contained in balls of radii
R,R_tilde. Let S=T_tilde T^(-1). Comparing widths in each direction
gives

    ||S||<=R_tilde/rho,      ||S^(-1)||<=R/rho_tilde.

The fine-coordinate diagonal block of S is A_tilde A^(-1), and that
of its inverse is A A_tilde^(-1). Their operator norms are at most
the corresponding full operator norms. Covering radii therefore obey

    (rho_tilde/R) coveringradius(A Lambda)
       <= coveringradius(A_tilde Lambda)
       <= (R_tilde/rho) coveringradius(A Lambda).

Indeed applying a linear map to a nearest-lattice-point displacement
multiplies its norm by at most the map's operator norm; applying the
inverse gives the reverse inequality. Uniformly round normalizations
have fixed bounds on these four radii. Such bounds hold for the
normalized anchor construction above. Thus (4), or its failure along
a subsequence, cannot be repaired merely by choosing a different
uniformly round block normalization of that same component.

## 3. Actual residual fine cosets and the exact Jacobian identity

Write g_(l,z)=(g^u_(l,z),g^x_(l,z)). The original fine condition
u in Lambda_l+a_l becomes, in the residual coordinates w=(U,X),

    U in A_(l,i)(Lambda_l+a_l)-g^u_(l,z).                 (7)

These offsets may depend on z even within a component. Their lattice
part has component-dependent covolume

    v_(l,i)=v_l |det A_(l,i)|.                           (8)

On a fixed original fine fiber, X=B_(l,i)u+C_(l,i)x-g^x_(l,z).
The s-dimensional continuous Jacobian is |det C_(l,i)|. Therefore

    v_(l,i) H_s(residual fine section)
             =(v_l/M_l) H_s(original fine section).      (9)

This identity is also valid for s=0 with determinant one in that
zero-dimensional block. A translation of the coset does not affect
its covolume or covering radius.

Define sigma_l on the fine subset of B_l by summing, in each residual
z-fiber, its H_s fine sections on (7), multiplied by v_(l,i). The
fixed orthogonal embedding of the residual m-block is isometric, so
it adds no H_s factor. Formula (9) proves the exact pushforward

    (F_l)_# sigma_l=mu_l/M_l,
    sigma_l(total)=mu_l(total)/M_l.                      (10)

There is no common fine lattice or common fine covolume across the
whole lift in this definition. It is an auxiliary finite weighted
measure, not an unweighted mixed-volume source to which OC is applied.

## 4. Uniform sampling in the bounded residual coordinates

Choose R with R_(l,z) subset [-R,R]^m. A measurable Voronoi cell
of A_(l,i)Lambda_l lies in the Euclidean ball of radius rho_(l,i),
and hence in the coordinate cube of that radius. The uniform
convex-set sampling lemma from
`candidate 0639bd50a01557c4`
applies to every translate of that lattice and gives

    error_(l,i)=2r rho_(l,i)(2R+2rho_(l,i))^(m-1).        (11)

It includes empty and lower-dimensional cuts and closed-boundary
mass. A lifted ambient halfspace restricts to an affine halfspace,
the whole space, or the empty set on each residual m-plane. Thus,
with e_l=sum_i |P_i| error_(l,i),

    sup_(closed halfspaces H) |sigma_l(H)-nu_l(H)|<=e_l,
    |sigma_l(total)-1|<=e_l ->0.                         (12)

The same conclusion applies to total mass by taking the whole source.
Once e_l<1, normalization yields, uniformly over ALL halfspaces,

    |sigma_l(H)/sigma_l(total)-nu_l(H)|
                                  <=2e_l/(1-e_l).        (13)

In particular mu_l(total)>0 and mu_l(total)/M_l->1. This is uniform
halfspace discrepancy, not total-variation convergence between the
singular sampled measure and the continuum lift.

## 5. A deterministic fine point in the selected residual fiber

Fix a limiting lift point of depth arbitrarily close to
max depth_(nu_*), at coarse base z in component i. The full-shape
theorem proves continuity as this point moves within its own
residual m-fiber: component indicators are represented by affine
graph features, so every component cut can be extended to exclude
all other components. Consequently full-lift depth on component i
equals its mass times its normalized component depth. A common-block
section-volume bound then gives a uniform Lipschitz estimate for
motion inside that component.

Move the chosen point an arbitrarily small distance into int R_z,
losing arbitrarily little limiting depth, and call its residual
coordinate w=(U,X). Hausdorff convergence to the positive body R_z
puts a fixed ball w+eta B_2^m inside R_(l,z) for all large l.
Choose a closest point U_l to U in the actual coset (7); then

    |U_l-U|<=rho_(l,i) ->0.

Keep X fixed. The point w_l=(U_l,X) lies in R_(l,z) eventually and
is an actual fine point of the lift. The original point F_l(w_l)
has u in Lambda_l+a_l by (7), and belongs to K_(l,z) by (6). Thus
it lies in the ORIGINAL fine mixed source. No rounding after an
uncontrolled inverse map is being inferred.

Total-variation convergence of the full residual volume measures in
their fixed m-planes gives uniform halfspace-mass convergence
nu_l->nu_*. The component Lipschitz estimate just described handles
the displacement w_l-w. Hence nu_l-depth at w_l tends to the depth
of the selected limiting interior point. Equation (13) transfers
that lower bound to normalized sigma_l-depth at the SAME feasible
point. Finally every original halfspace containing F_l(w_l) pulls
back to a containing lifted halfspace or the whole source; (10)
gives exact equality of its normalized mass. Therefore

    depth_(mu_l)(F_l(w_l))
                >=depth_(sigma_l/sigma_l(total))(w_l).

Let the initial interior perturbation and maximal-depth error tend
to zero. This proves (5), including all closed and purely base cuts.

## 6. Discarding coarse-zero-weight fibers needs a FINE-mass condition

If some coarse relative masses tend to zero, retain P_+ as in the
full-shape theorem. It is lattice-convex. Normalize its component
maps by its own coarse mass M_(l,+), and assume (4) for every retained
component. The preceding proof gives

    mu_(l,+)(total)/M_(l,+) ->1.

Let mu_(l,-) be the actual fine measure on the omitted coarse bases.
For a recovery point in the retained source, restriction only lowers
unnormalized cap masses, so the exact comparison is

    depth_(mu_l)(y)
       >=[mu_(l,+)(total)/mu_l(total)]
                             depth_(mu_(l,+))(y).        (14)

Thus the conclusion (5) for the FULL fine source requires, for example,

    mu_(l,-)(total)/M_(l,+) ->0.                         (15)

More generally a limiting retained fine mass fraction theta gives
the lower bound theta times the maximal limiting lift depth. If
limsup mu_(l,-)(total)/M_(l,+)<=R_0<infinity, the factor is at least
1/(1+R_0). Coarse weight zero alone does not imply (15).

For an exact warning, keep the thin Q_0 of the crossed-triangle note
with epsilon=h^2 but replace Q_1 by the segment {u=0,-1<=x<=1}.
All vertices are sampled and the hull still contains the fixed full
tetrahedron. The omitted coarse area is zero, but its fine mass is
2h, compared with retained coarse mass 2h^2. The retained Q_0 block
normalization leaves fine mesh h tending to zero. Thus even that
retained-component mesh condition does not make omitted fine mass
negligible. This example establishes the missing mass comparison,
not a failure of a sharp depth theorem.

## 7. Conditional lower-rank consequence

For full-rank P, the compact full-shape lift has continuous ambient
dimension D<=B(k,m):=(m+1)2^k-k-1, with intrinsic fiber dimension m.
If OC is established at the relevant lower integer ranks and these
continuous ambient dimensions, including intrinsic intersections,
then its limiting depth is at least 2^(-k)Gamma_(B(k,m)). For a
retained lower-rank support, apply the saturated coarse lattice
reduction first; this only improves the same displayed lower bound.
Under (4) and, when needed, (15), (5) transfers that bound to the
liminf of the original fine depths.

For a full-sequence liminf, first choose any subsequence realizing
that liminf and then take the compact full-shape subsequence used
above. The same universal dimension bound applies to every such
extracted limit, proving the stated lower bound for the original
sequence, rather than only for one favored subsequence.

For s>=1 this is strictly larger than 2^(-k-r)Gamma_s, since every
Gamma_D>1/4, Gamma_s<=1/2, and 2^r>=2. The same strict comparison
holds for s=0,r>=2. The case s=0,r=1 is not concluded by this strict
comparison alone. For k=0 the sole coarse theorem invoked is ordinary
continuous Grunbaum. This paragraph is a CONDITIONAL implication;
neither the necessary lower-rank OC theorem nor (4) is assumed proved
for arbitrary instances.

## 8. Strict improvement over the original relative-mesh hypothesis

There are uniformly round, exact fine-hull sequences with
delta_l/M_l->infinity that satisfy (4). Choose integers L divisible
by three tending to infinity and put

    h=L^(-2),      epsilon=h^2=L^(-4),      a=L^(-1).

Take Q_0 as before and replace Q_1 by

    conv{(-a,-1),(a,1),(0,2epsilon/a)}.                  (16)

Both areas are 2epsilon, and all fine u-vertices lie in hZ. The
baseline tetrahedron is the shear u<-u+a x of the fixed tetrahedron,
so the same fixed inner/outer-ball argument applies. Its original
delta/M ratio is h/(8epsilon)=L^2/8, tending to infinity.

Determinant-1/M block maps are

    Q_0: U=u,       X=x/(4epsilon),
    Q_1: U=u/(2a),  X=a(x-u/a)/(2epsilon).               (17)

They send the fibers to fixed area-1/2 triangles. Their fine spacings
are h and h/(2a)=1/(2L), both tending to zero. Hence (4) holds.
The sampled second-fiber mass is exactly 2epsilon: writing N=a/h=L,
the tent sum sum_(i=-N)^N(1-|i|/N)=N gives this identity. The first
mass is epsilon(2+h), as before. Uniform sampling in the two fixed
triangles, and isolation of the two coarse bases, show their global
fine maximal depth tends to 2/9. In contrast, the choice a=h in
the obstruction note has a permanently non-dense second component
and limiting fine maximal depth 1/4.

The exact block determinants, transformed meshes, and finite tent
sums in this comparison are checked in
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_transformed_component_mesh_recovery.py`.
